title: Visitor and Bell
premise: Sable Vasquez, a meticulous new teacher at Hollow Creek Elementary, notices that certain students vanish from her rosters mid-semester and that no one else remembers them. Her documentation leads her to the town's founding ledger, where she learns the school sits on a covenant: each generation must 'invite in' a visitor to keep the valley prosperous. When Sable refuses to sign herself into the ritual, the house she rents begins reflecting rooms one second late—the Visitor arriving ahead of its own image—and she realizes the missing children were never taken; they were traded by parents who chose duty over love. In the final hours before sunrise, Sable burns the ledger and offers the Visitor her own name freely given rather than coerced, breaking the covenant's logic of sacrifice; the mirrors catch up, the children return with memories intact, and the town's prosperity collapses—but justice, outside any law, is finally done.
about_author: S. M. Vane is the pen name of a former night-shift archivist who spent years cataloging institutional records from defunct schools and asylums. They write horror about paperwork, memory, and the quiet violence of small-town complicity.

chapters.title: The Roster That Breathes
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Arriving in Hollow Creek, Sable documents everything—class lists, odd silences, a classroom desk carved with names that aren't on any roster. A student named Wren mentions 'the girl who used to sit there,' then goes pale when asked. The emotional beat is creeping unease: Sable's habit of recording feels like safety, but the school's staff watch her notebook with something like hunger.

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. At home, every mirror reflects the room one second late—a spoon falls before it drops. Cross-referencing old yearbooks against enrollment records, Sable finds seven students erased mid-semester across decades, all children of families who prospered afterward. She confronts Principal Aldous, who gently explains 'traditions.' The beat shifts from unease to dread: staying invisible was never an option; they've been waiting for a newcomer without local ties.

chapters.title: What Was Invited
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, intercut with Wren's diary entries. Sable finds the founding ledger in the school basement: the covenant, the invitation rite, and her own name already inked in by someone—Aldous forged her consent. The Visitor manifests through reflections, wearing the faces of the missing children. Wren, whose mother signed her away, helps Sable steal the ledger. The beat is betrayal curdling into resolve: love against duty made flesh in a child choosing Sable over her own mother.

chapters.title: Sunrise, Freely Given
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Barricaded until dawn, Sable refuses to run: instead she speaks the Visitor's true name from the ledger's first page and offers herself willingly—not as sacrifice but as witness, asking it to remember what was done in its name. The covenant, built on coercion, cannot hold a free gift; the mirrors sync, the children wake in the cornfield, and the ledger burns. The beat is cathartic justice: the town loses its fortune, Sable stays to teach the returned, and the last mirror shows only the present.
